text.p: Conrail Inc. shareholders derailed a planned $9.3 billion railroad merger with CSX Corp. Friday with a thumping rejection of a key provision to let the deal proceed.
The vote handed a victory to Norfolk Southern Corp., which is pursuing a rival $10.3 billion bid for Conrail.
But it also created at least a temporary stalemate in which neither side can complete a deal, and all three companies are determined not to give up.

"It is clearly the Conrail board's intent to see through the CSX-Conrail merger," Conrail Chairman David LeVan said in announcing the defeat at a news conference. The company will not agree to a deal with Norfolk Southern, he said.
Norfolk Southern Chairman David Goode said, "Now that the shareholders have spoken, it is time for Conrail's board to accept their will. ... Whatever happens, we will move forward."

The measure rejected by Conrail shareholders would have exempted Conrail from a Pennsylvania law that would require CSX to pay all cash for Conrail once its stake in the Philadelphia-based railroad reached 20 percent.

The measure was rejected by at least 53 percent of all outstanding shares, including more than 90 percent of those not held by CSX or by Conrail employees, Goode said. He was citing shareholder proxies received by Norfolk Southern.
He termed the vote margin "overwhelming."
The results were preliminary. Official results will not be released for several days.
The rejection prevents Richmond, Va.-based CSX from closing on a $110-per-share tender offer to raise its stake in Conrail to 40 percent from 19.9 percent.
The offer, scheduled to close Jan. 22, would have given effective control over Conrail to CSX, which holds an option for additional shares.
But Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern also is stymied, by an agreement between Conrail and CSX not to talk to other possible partners without each other's permission until 1999.
Asked whether he could wait two years, Goode said, "We will not go away. We're going to be in this transaction. We're going to make it happen."
Asked whether he was willing to pay more if needed to respond to a new CSX bid, Goode said, "We'll look at anything that happens in terms of the right move at the right time."
Goode said he was willing to discuss a deal with Conrail and CSX, but talks could go forward only on the basis of Norfolk Southern's $115-per-share cash offer.
CSX agreed to pay 40 percent cash and 60 percent stock for Conrail in a deal worth a total of about $104 per share before Friday's vote.
Conrail stock was unchanged at $103.50 on the New York Stock Exchange. CSX rose $1.75 to $46.75 and Norfolk Southern dropped 12.5 cents to $88, also on the NYSE.
LeVan said he would talk to Norfolk Southern, but only about issues such as granting competitive access to Conrail-CSX routes.
Another shareholder vote will be scheduled, LeVan said. "We will reschedule a meeting. We will move on. ... We obviously have to get out and sell the value of this transaction," he said.
He attributed the defeat to a Norfolk Southern statement Monday that it would buy 9.9 percent of Conrail for $115 per share. That tender offer will be launched as soon as possible, Goode said.
LeVan also said the company would re-evaluate the deal's structure, but he said he believed the defeated deal "is clearly fairly valued." CSX has said it was unwilling to further raise its bid.
CSX said it was confident it would prevail.

"We have no intention of amending or altering our merger agreement in any way in light of this apparent vote," CSX Chairman John Snow said. He said the managements of CSX and Conrail were preparing to present the merger to the federal Surface Transportation Board (STB) in March.

Norfolk Southern plans to present its own proposal to the boards in early March, Goode said. The agency has said it could strike the two-year "exclusivity" period if it approves a deal with Norfolk Southern, but Conrail said the agency cannot force a merger against Conrail's will.

A takeover stock trader active in the deal said one way to a resolution would be for the three railroads to agree to a deal that may essentially "carve up" Conrail, but with Conrail's involvement and consent.
"I think what's going to happen is, there's going to be a meeting," he said. "It has to be all three parties."

Support for Conrail was strong at the shareholders meeting, at which speakers were almost all long-term Conrail employees who endorsed the CSX merger. Institutional shareholders, who own the majority of Conrail shares, usually vote by proxy and are not present at shareholder meetings.
LeVan said hearing such statements from the employees reinforced his commitment "to doing everything I can possibly do to see that the CSX merger is accomplished."
